transitivity: both — transitive (breathe clean air), intransitive (she breathed slowly)
gloss: To take air into your lungs and let it out again.
examples: *Breathe* in through your nose and out through your mouth.
She *breathed* a little easier once the fever broke.
He was *breathing* hard by the time he reached the top floor.
contrast: The noun is *breath* /brɛθ/, short vowel and voiceless *th*; the verb *breathe* /briːð/ has a long vowel and a voiced *th*. You take a *breath*, then you *breathe*.

transitivity: both — transitive (inhale the fumes), intransitive (inhale deeply)
gloss: To breathe air, smoke, or a smell into your lungs.
examples: *Inhale* deeply and hold it for three seconds.
He *inhaled* a lungful of smoke and started coughing.
The mask keeps you from *inhaling* dust.

transitivity: both — transitive (exhale the smoke), intransitive (exhale slowly)
gloss: To let air out of your lungs.
examples: *Exhale* slowly as you lower the weight.
She *exhaled* and finally let her shoulders drop.
The nurse asked him to keep *exhaling* into the tube.

gloss: To push air out of your throat with a sudden loud noise, usually because you are sick.
examples: He *coughs* all night when his allergies flare up.
She *coughed* so hard her chest hurt.
The baby has been *coughing* since Tuesday.
contrast: The *gh* is said as /f/: *cough* rhymes with *off*, not with *though*.

gloss: To suddenly blow air out through your nose and mouth in a way you cannot control.
examples: Pepper always makes me *sneeze*.
She *sneezed* three times in a row.
He kept *sneezing* all through the meeting.

gloss: To open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply because you are tired or bored.
examples: Try not to *yawn* while she is explaining it.
He *yawned* and looked at the clock.
Half the class was *yawning* by ten after eight.

gloss: To let out a long breath because you are tired, sad, or relieved.
examples: Don't *sigh* like that — it wasn't that bad.
She *sighed* and put the phone down.
He was *sighing* over the bill the whole evening.
contrast: The *gh* is silent: *sigh* rhymes with *my*, and the past *sighed* rhymes with *side*.

gloss: To breathe in suddenly and loudly, from shock or from a lack of air.
examples: The cold water made her *gasp*.
He *gasped* when he saw the hospital bill.
She came up out of the pool *gasping* for air.

gloss: To breathe in quick short breaths after hard exercise or in heat.
examples: The dog starts to *pant* the second we go outside.
She *panted* up the last flight of stairs.
He was *panting* too hard to answer me.

gloss: To breathe with a rough whistling sound, usually because of asthma or a chest infection.
examples: He tends to *wheeze* in cold air.
She *wheezed* through the whole night.
The doctor listened to his chest while he was *wheezing*.

gloss: To breathe with a loud rough noise while you are asleep.
examples: My husband *snores* every single night.
He *snored* through the entire movie.
I couldn't sleep with someone *snoring* next to me.

transitivity: both — transitive (the fumes choked him), intransitive (she choked on a bone)
gloss: To be unable to breathe because something is blocking your throat, or to stop someone else from breathing.
examples: Cut the grapes so the baby doesn't *choke*.
He *choked* on a piece of steak at dinner.
The smoke left us *choking* in the hallway.
contrast: A person *chokes on* food — the preposition is *on*, not 'with'.

transitivity: both — transitive (the smoke suffocated them), intransitive (he nearly suffocated)
gloss: To die or almost die because you cannot get any air.
examples: A plastic bag can *suffocate* a small child.
Two people *suffocated* in the smoke before the crew arrived.
The heat in that attic is *suffocating*.

transitivity: both — transitive (relax your grip), intransitive (relax on the couch)
gloss: To stop being tense and let your body and mind rest.
examples: *Relax* your shoulders and let your arms hang.
We *relaxed* by the pool all afternoon.
She was finally *relaxing* when the phone rang.
contrast: A verb ending in *-x* takes *-es* in the third person: *relaxes*, never 'relaxs'.

gloss: To sleep for a short time during the day.
examples: I *nap* for twenty minutes after lunch.
The baby *napped* in the car the whole way home.
He was *napping* on the couch when we got in.
contrast: One syllable, one vowel, one final consonant — so the *p* doubles: *napped*, *napping*.

gloss: To sleep lightly, often without meaning to.
examples: Grandpa likes to *doze* in his chair after dinner.
She *dozed* through most of the flight.
He was *dozing* with the TV still on.

transitivity: both — transitive (snooze the alarm), intransitive (snooze for an hour)
gloss: To sleep lightly for a short while, or to push the alarm back for a few more minutes.
examples: I always *snooze* the alarm twice.
He *snoozed* on the train and missed his stop.
She was *snoozing* in the sun on the back steps.

transitivity: both — transitive (the climb tired us), intransitive (he tires easily)
gloss: To become tired, or to make someone tired.
examples: Stairs *tire* him more than they used to.
She *tired* quickly in the weeks after surgery.
The heat was *tiring* the runners before the halfway mark.

gloss: To make someone completely tired, or to use something up entirely.
examples: Night shifts *exhaust* her.
The twelve-hour drive *exhausted* all of us.
We have *exhausted* every other treatment.
contrast: The *x* here is said /ɡz/ and the *h* is silent: ig-ZAWST.

gloss: To get your strength and health back after an illness or a hard effort.
examples: It takes a week to *recuperate* from that kind of flu.
He *recuperated* at his sister's place for a month.
She is still *recuperating* from the operation.

transitivity: both — transitive (revive a patient), intransitive (the plant revived)
gloss: To bring someone back to consciousness, or to come back to life or strength.
examples: Paramedics can sometimes *revive* a patient after several minutes.
Cold water *revived* her a little.
He was *revived* at the scene and rushed to the hospital.

transitivity: both — transitive (exercise the dog), intransitive (exercise every morning)
gloss: To move your body in order to stay fit and healthy.
examples: Try to *exercise* three times a week.
He *exercised* every morning for a year.
She has been *exercising* since her doctor warned her.

transitivity: both — transitive (stretch your hamstrings), intransitive (stretch before a run)
gloss: To make your muscles longer by pulling on them gently.
examples: *Stretch* before you run, not after.
She *stretched* her calves against the wall.
He stood up, *stretching* his arms over his head.

gloss: To run slowly and steadily for exercise.
examples: We *jog* along the river on Sundays.
She *jogged* two miles before breakfast.
He hurt his knee *jogging* on pavement.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *jogged*, *jogging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (train young athletes), intransitive (train for a race)
gloss: To practice regularly to get fit or to get better at a sport.
examples: He *trains* six days a week.
She *trained* for a year before the marathon.
They have been *training* with a new coach since spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (lift a box), intransitive (he lifts at the gym)
gloss: To raise something heavy off the ground, often as exercise.
examples: Bend your knees when you *lift* anything heavy.
He *lifted* weights all through college.
She threw her back out *lifting* a suitcase.

gloss: To bend a joint or tighten a muscle.
examples: *Flex* your foot toward your knee and hold it.
He *flexed* his arm to show me the bruise.
The therapist watched her *flexing* her fingers.

gloss: To lower your body by bending your knees while keeping your back straight.
examples: *Squat* down and lift with your legs.
He *squatted* beside the bed to talk to her.
She was *squatting* to pick up the baby when her back gave out.
contrast: The *t* doubles: *squatted*, *squatting*.

gloss: To run as fast as you can over a short distance.
examples: We *sprint* the last hundred meters.
He *sprinted* for the bus and still missed it.
She pulled a muscle *sprinting* on cold legs.

transitivity: both — transitive (jump the fence), intransitive (jump up and down)
gloss: To push yourself off the ground with your legs.
examples: *Jump* as high as you can and land softly.
The dog *jumped* right over the fence.
He landed badly *jumping* off the wall.

gloss: To move along on your hands and knees.
examples: Most babies *crawl* before they walk.
She *crawled* under the table to get the phone.
He was *crawling* around the yard with the kids.

gloss: To walk unevenly because one leg or foot hurts.
examples: You still *limp* a little on that ankle.
He *limped* off the field on his own.
She has been *limping* since the fall.

gloss: To catch your foot on something and almost fall.
examples: People *stumble* on that step all the time.
He *stumbled* over the curb and dropped his coffee.
She kept *stumbling* in the dark hallway.

transitivity: both — transitive (he tripped his brother), intransitive (she tripped on a root)
gloss: To catch your foot on something so that you fall or nearly fall.
examples: Be careful you don't *trip* on that cord.
He *tripped* and landed hard on his wrist.
She was *tripping* over her own feet by mile twenty.
contrast: The *p* doubles: *tripped*, *tripping*. You *trip over* or *trip on* something.

gloss: To walk unsteadily, as though you are about to fall.
examples: People *stagger* a little when their blood pressure drops.
He *staggered* to the couch and sat down.
She was *staggering* by the end of the shift.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, so the *r* does not double: *staggered*, *staggering*.

gloss: To close and open your eyes quickly.
examples: Try not to *blink* while I put the drops in.
He *blinked* hard against the bright light.
She sat there *blinking*, still half asleep.

transitivity: both — transitive (nod your head), intransitive (he nodded politely)
gloss: To move your head down and up to say yes or to greet someone.
examples: Just *nod* if you understand what I'm asking.
She *nodded* and took the prescription.
He was *nodding* along to everything the doctor said.
contrast: The *d* doubles: *nodded*, *nodding*.

transitivity: both — transitive (shrug your shoulders), intransitive (he just shrugged)
gloss: To raise your shoulders to show that you do not know or do not care.
examples: Don't just *shrug* — tell me where it hurts.
He *shrugged* and looked at the floor.
She answered by *shrugging* her shoulders.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *shrugged*, *shrugging*.

gloss: To move your eyebrows down because you are worried, thinking, or in pain.
examples: You *frown* every time you stand up — does your knee hurt?
The doctor *frowned* at the x-ray.
He was *frowning* at the label, trying to read the dose.

gloss: To become red in the face from embarrassment.
examples: I *blush* whenever anyone looks at me.
She *blushed* when he thanked her in front of everyone.
He was *blushing* right up to his ears.

transitivity: both — transitive (chew your food), intransitive (chew slowly)
gloss: To break food up with your teeth.
examples: *Chew* slowly or your stomach will hurt.
He *chewed* the pill instead of swallowing it.
She was *chewing* gum through the whole appointment.

transitivity: both — transitive (swallow the pill), intransitive (it hurts to swallow)
gloss: To make food, drink, or medicine go down your throat.
examples: *Swallow* the tablet with a full glass of water.
It hurt every time she *swallowed*.
He nearly choked *swallowing* a bite that big.

transitivity: both — transitive (digest lactose), intransitive (food digests slowly)
gloss: To break food down in your stomach so that your body can use it.
examples: Some people can't *digest* milk at all.
He *digested* the meal badly and felt sick all evening.
Fat is *digested* far more slowly than sugar.

transitivity: both — transitive (sniff the milk), intransitive (he sniffed and wiped his nose)
gloss: To breathe in through your nose, to smell something or because your nose is running.
examples: *Sniff* this and tell me if it smells off.
She *sniffed* and reached for a tissue.
He has been *sniffing* and coughing all week.

transitivity: both — transitive (scratch your arm), intransitive (don't scratch)
gloss: To rub your skin with your nails, or to make a thin cut on a surface.
examples: Try not to *scratch* the bite.
The cat *scratched* her arm badly.
He woke up *scratching* his legs again.

gloss: To move your hand back and forth over a part of the body or a surface.
examples: *Rub* the cream in until it disappears.
She *rubbed* her eyes and sat up.
He was *rubbing* his shoulder where it hurt.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *rubbed*, *rubbing*.

gloss: To press something firmly, usually with your hand.
examples: *Squeeze* my hand if the pain gets worse.
The nurse *squeezed* his finger to get a drop of blood.
She was *squeezing* a stress ball the whole appointment.

gloss: To press someone's skin tightly between your finger and thumb.
examples: *Pinch* the skin and slide the needle in at an angle.
The new shoes *pinched* her heel raw.
He kept *pinching* the bridge of his nose to stop the bleeding.

gloss: To make a sudden face because of pain.
examples: Tell me where you *wince* when I press.
She *winced* as the doctor touched the bruise.
He was *wincing* with every step.

gloss: To move back suddenly because you are afraid of being hurt.
examples: Most kids *flinch* when they see the needle.
She *flinched* away from the bright light.
He took the shot without *flinching*.

gloss: To shake slightly because you are cold or feverish.
examples: You *shiver* like that when your fever is climbing.
She *shivered* under two blankets.
He was *shivering* in the waiting room.

gloss: To shake in a way you cannot control, from fear, cold, or weakness.
examples: My hands *tremble* when my blood sugar drops.
Her voice *trembled* when she read the results.
He was *trembling* so hard he couldn't hold the cup.

gloss: To shake for a moment from cold, fear, or disgust.
examples: I *shudder* just thinking about that surgery.
She *shuddered* and pulled the blanket up.
He was still *shuddering* an hour after the fall.

gloss: To make a long low sound because of pain or unhappiness.
examples: Don't *groan* — it is only a flu shot.
He *groaned* and rolled onto his side.
She was *groaning* in her sleep.
contrast: *Groaned* sounds exactly like *grown*, the participle of *grow* — one is a sound of pain, the other is getting bigger.

gloss: To make a long low sound of pain or complaint.
examples: Patients often *moan* as the anesthetic wears off.
He *moaned* softly and asked for water.
She was *moaning* about her back all afternoon.

transitivity: both — transitive (burp the baby), intransitive (he burped loudly)
gloss: To let air come up loudly from your stomach through your mouth.
examples: Babies have to *burp* after every bottle.
He *burped* and apologized.
She was *burping* the baby over her shoulder.

gloss: To hurt with a dull steady pain.
examples: My knees *ache* before it rains.
Her head *ached* all day.
He went to bed with every muscle *aching*.
contrast: The *ch* is said /k/: *ache* rhymes with *make*, not with *catch*.

gloss: To hurt in a steady beating rhythm.
examples: My finger *throbs* every time I lower my hand.
His tooth *throbbed* all night.
She woke up with a *throbbing* headache.
contrast: The *b* doubles: *throbbed*, *throbbing*.

gloss: To have a feeling on your skin that makes you want to scratch.
examples: Does the rash *itch* or burn?
The stitches *itched* for a week.
He couldn't sleep with his back *itching* like that.

gloss: To lose consciousness for a short time.
examples: Some people *faint* at the sight of blood.
She *fainted* in the shower and cut her forehead.
He has *fainted* twice this month.

gloss: To fall down suddenly because you are ill or very weak.
examples: Runners sometimes *collapse* in this kind of heat.
He *collapsed* at work and went out by ambulance.
She has *collapsed* twice since starting the new medication.

transitivity: both — transitive (vomit blood), intransitive (he vomited twice)
gloss: To bring food up from your stomach and out through your mouth.
examples: Call us if she starts to *vomit* again.
He *vomited* twice during the night.
The baby has been *vomiting* since morning.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *vomited*, *vomiting*.

transitivity: both — transitive (smoking worsens asthma), intransitive (the pain worsened)
gloss: To become worse, or to make something worse.
examples: Her symptoms usually *worsen* at night.
The cough *worsened* over the weekend.
Smoking is *worsening* his asthma.

transitivity: both — transitive (the infection weakened her heart), intransitive (he weakened quickly)
gloss: To become less strong, or to make something less strong.
examples: Weeks of bed rest can *weaken* your muscles fast.
The infection *weakened* her heart.
He has been *weakening* for months.

transitivity: both — transitive (strengthen your back), intransitive (the joint strengthened over time)
gloss: To make something stronger, or to become stronger.
examples: These exercises *strengthen* your lower back.
Physical therapy *strengthened* the knee enough to walk on.
She is *strengthening* her core before the season starts.

gloss: To pass a disease to a person, an animal, or a wound.
examples: One sick child can *infect* the whole class.
He *infected* half the office before he stayed home.
The cut got *infected* within two days.

gloss: To become ill again after you seemed to be getting better.
examples: About a third of patients *relapse* within a year.
He *relapsed* two months after the treatment ended.
She is terrified of *relapsing* again.
contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable, ri-LAPS; the noun *a relapse* is often REE-laps.

transitivity: both — transitive (survive the surgery), intransitive (only two survived)
gloss: To stay alive through an illness, an accident, or a dangerous situation.
examples: Most people *survive* this kind of surgery without trouble.
He *survived* the crash with a broken arm.
She has *survived* two rounds of chemotherapy.

transitivity: both — transitive (stress ages the skin), intransitive (he aged quickly)
gloss: To grow older, or to make someone look older.
examples: Some people *age* more slowly than others.
He has *aged* ten years since the diagnosis.
Smoking is *aging* her skin.
contrast: American English drops the *e*: *aging*. British English writes *ageing*.

gloss: To produce sweat, especially when you are hot or nervous.
examples: Athletes *perspire* much more in humid weather.
He *perspired* through his shirt during the exam.
She was *perspiring* heavily and looked pale.

gloss: To catch a serious illness.
examples: Workers can *contract* the virus from contaminated water.
He *contracted* pneumonia in the hospital.
She had *contracted* the infection weeks before any symptoms showed.
contrast: As a verb the stress is on the second syllable, kuhn-TRAKT. The noun *a contract* (a legal agreement) is KAHN-trakt.

gloss: To keep a person or animal away from others so a disease cannot spread.
examples: The shelter *quarantines* every new dog for ten days.
He was *quarantined* for two weeks after the trip.
The hospital is *quarantining* the whole floor.

transitivity: both — transitive (starve yourself), intransitive (the animals starved)
gloss: To suffer or die from not having enough food.
examples: You can't *starve* yourself and call it a diet.
The dog had nearly *starved* before they found him.
He said he was *starving* and ate three plates.

gloss: To go without food for a set period, for medical or religious reasons.
examples: You have to *fast* for twelve hours before the blood test.
She *fasted* all day and felt light-headed by evening.
He has been *fasting* two days a week since January.
contrast: Spelled like the adjective *fast* (quick), but the verb means to eat nothing at all.

gloss: To eat less or eat carefully in order to lose weight.
examples: She *diets* every January and quits by March.
He *dieted* for six months before the wedding.
*Dieting* without exercise rarely works for long.

gloss: To eat small amounts of food between meals.
examples: I *snack* all afternoon when I'm bored.
He *snacked* on almonds instead of chips.
She has been *snacking* less since she started writing it down.

transitivity: both — transitive (smoke a cigarette), intransitive (he smokes)
gloss: To breathe in smoke from a cigarette, cigar, or pipe.
examples: He *smokes* half a pack a day.
She *smoked* for twenty years and quit at forty.
He got sick of *smoking* outside in the cold.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sun tanned his arms), intransitive (she tans easily)
gloss: To make your skin darker by staying in the sun.
examples: Some people burn, others just *tan*.
She *tanned* easily even as a kid.
He spent the week *tanning* on the beach and paid for it later.
contrast: The *n* doubles: *tanned*, *tanning*.

gloss: To hurt a part of someone's body in an accident.
examples: Bad form can *injure* your lower back in one rep.
He *injured* his shoulder in the second game.
Four people were *injured* in the crash.

gloss: To injure someone, usually by cutting or shooting.
examples: A knife can *wound* deeply without much blood.
The bullet *wounded* her in the leg.
He was *wounded* twice during his tour.
contrast: Say WOOND for the injury word. The identical spelling *wound* /waʊnd/ (WOWND) is the past of *wind* (to wind a clock).

transitivity: both — transitive (bruise your hip), intransitive (she bruises easily)
gloss: To make a purple mark on the skin by hitting or pressing it.
examples: I *bruise* easily on this medication.
She *bruised* her hip on the edge of the table.
His arm is still *bruising* from the IV.
contrast: Spelled *-uise* but said BROOZ, rhyming with *lose*.

gloss: To rub the skin off part of your body against a rough surface.
examples: Kids *scrape* their knees all summer.
He *scraped* his elbow on the pavement.
She came home with both palms *scraped* raw.

gloss: To injure a joint by twisting it badly.
examples: You can *sprain* an ankle just stepping off a curb.
She *sprained* her wrist catching herself.
He has *sprained* the same ankle three times.
contrast: A *sprain* damages the ligaments around a joint, a *strain* pulls a muscle, and a *fracture* breaks the bone.

transitivity: both — transitive (twist your ankle), intransitive (the cord twists)
gloss: To turn a joint too far and hurt it.
examples: Don't *twist* your knee when you turn.
He *twisted* his ankle on the last stair.
She played three more holes on a *twisted* knee.

gloss: To injure a muscle by stretching or working it too hard.
examples: Lifting like that will *strain* your back.
He *strained* a hamstring in warm-ups.
She is resting a *strained* shoulder.

transitivity: both — transitive (fracture a rib), intransitive (the bone fractured)
gloss: To crack or break a bone.
examples: A fall like that can *fracture* a hip.
He *fractured* two ribs in the accident.
She is still in a boot with a *fractured* foot.

gloss: To push a bone out of its normal place at a joint.
examples: Throwing that hard can *dislocate* a shoulder.
He *dislocated* his finger catching the ball.
She has *dislocated* the same shoulder twice.

gloss: To hurt a person or damage their health.
examples: One glass of wine won't *harm* you.
The drug *harmed* more patients than it helped.
No one was *harmed* in the accident.

gloss: To hurt something so that it no longer works properly.
examples: Loud music can *damage* your hearing permanently.
The fever *damaged* his kidneys.
Years of sun had *damaged* her skin badly.

gloss: To harm or kill someone with a substance that is dangerous to the body.
examples: Old paint can *poison* a small child.
The fumes *poisoned* two workers.
He was *poisoned* by something he ate at the picnic.

transitivity: both — transitive (the burn scarred his arm), intransitive (deep cuts scar)
gloss: To leave a permanent mark on the skin after a wound heals.
examples: Deep cuts almost always *scar*.
The burn *scarred* his forearm.
Her knee is badly *scarred* from the surgery.
contrast: The *r* doubles: *scarred*, *scarring* — one *r* would give *scared* (frightened), a different word.

transitivity: both — transitive (heal a wound), intransitive (the cut healed)
gloss: To become healthy again, or to make a wound or a person healthy again.
examples: Small cuts *heal* in a few days.
The break *healed* crookedly and had to be reset.
Her shoulder is still *healing*.
contrast: *Heal* sounds exactly like *heel*, the back of your foot.

gloss: To make an illness go away completely.
examples: Antibiotics *cure* most ear infections.
The treatment *cured* him in three weeks.
Nothing has ever *cured* her migraines.
contrast: You *cure* a person *of* a disease, and you look for a cure *for* a disease.

gloss: To give a patient medical care for an illness or injury.
examples: They *treat* burns in the unit upstairs.
The doctor *treated* her for pneumonia.
He is being *treated* with a new drug.
contrast: You *treat* someone *for* an illness *with* a medicine. Treating an illness is not the same as curing it.

gloss: To look at a patient carefully in order to find out what is wrong.
examples: The doctor will *examine* your throat first.
A nurse *examined* the wound and changed the dressing.
He was *examined* twice before anyone found the fracture.

gloss: To identify what illness someone has.
examples: It can take years to *diagnose* this condition.
They *diagnosed* her with diabetes at thirty.
He was *diagnosed* last spring.
contrast: You *diagnose* a person *with* a disease, or *diagnose* the disease itself — never 'diagnose a person of'.

gloss: To officially tell a patient to take a certain medicine or treatment.
examples: Doctors rarely *prescribe* antibiotics for a cold.
She *prescribed* something for the pain.
He has been *prescribed* two different inhalers.

transitivity: intransitive in the medical sense (operate on a patient)
gloss: To cut into a patient's body in order to repair or remove something.
examples: They will *operate* first thing in the morning.
The surgeon *operated* on her knee twice.
He is being *operated* on right now.
contrast: In the medical sense you *operate on* a patient. Without *on*, *operate* means to run a machine or a business.

gloss: To put medicine into the body with a needle.
examples: Diabetics *inject* insulin every day.
The nurse *injected* the dye before the scan.
He was *injecting* himself in the stomach.

gloss: To give someone a vaccine to protect them from a disease.
examples: Clinics *vaccinate* children against measles.
She *vaccinated* both kids last fall.
He has been *vaccinated* twice this year.
contrast: Two *c*s: *vaccinate*. You vaccinate someone *against* a disease.

gloss: To wrap a strip of cloth around a wound.
examples: *Bandage* it firmly, but not so tight the hand goes numb.
The medic *bandaged* his hand right there on the field.
She was *bandaging* her ankle when I came in.

gloss: To sew the edges of a wound together.
examples: They can *stitch* a cut like that in five minutes.
The doctor *stitched* the gash above his eye.
Her chin was *stitched* in the emergency room.

gloss: To clean something with a substance that kills germs.
examples: *Disinfect* the cut before you cover it.
She *disinfected* the counter after handling the chicken.
The room is *disinfected* between patients.

gloss: To make equipment completely free of germs, usually with heat or chemicals.
examples: Boil the bottles to *sterilize* them.
The nurse *sterilized* the instruments.
Everything on that tray has been *sterilized*.
contrast: American English spells it *-ize*: *sterilize*, *sterilized*. British English also allows *sterilise*.

gloss: To take care of someone who is sick or injured.
examples: Somebody has to *nurse* him through this.
She *nursed* her mother for two years.
He is at home *nursing* a broken rib.

gloss: To put someone in a hospital for treatment.
examples: They only *hospitalize* the worst cases.
He was *hospitalized* for a week with pneumonia.
Hundreds have been *hospitalized* this flu season.

gloss: To move an organ or piece of tissue from one body into another.
examples: Surgeons can now *transplant* a whole face.
They *transplanted* a kidney from his brother.
Her cornea was *transplanted* last year.
contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable, trans-PLANT; the noun *a transplant* stresses the first, TRANS-plant.

gloss: To give blood, an organ, or money in order to help someone.
examples: You can *donate* blood every eight weeks.
He *donated* a kidney to a stranger.
She has been *donating* plasma for years.

gloss: To officially let a patient leave the hospital.
examples: They usually *discharge* you the next morning.
She was *discharged* after two nights.
He is being *discharged* this afternoon.
contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable, dis-CHAHRJ; the noun *a discharge* stresses the first, DIS-chahrj.

gloss: To make pain or worry less strong.
examples: Honey will *soothe* a sore throat.
The cold cloth *soothed* her forehead.
He sat there *soothing* the baby for an hour.
contrast: Ends in *-the* with a voiced *th*, like *breathe*: the *th* of *this*, not of *think*.

gloss: To make someone feel less sad, frightened, or in pain.
examples: Nurses do more to *comfort* people than we give them credit for.
She *comforted* him while they waited for the results.
He was *comforting* his daughter out in the hallway.

transitivity: both — transitive (ease the swelling), intransitive (the pain eased)
gloss: To make pain or a problem less severe, or to become less severe.
examples: Ice will *ease* the swelling.
The medication *eased* the pain within an hour.
His breathing is *easing* now.

gloss: To make a part of the body lose feeling.
examples: They will *numb* the gum before they drill.
The cold *numbed* her fingers in minutes.
The dentist is *numbing* the whole side of his mouth.
contrast: The *b* is silent: NUM, like *thumb* and *dumb*.

gloss: To make someone stop being upset or frightened.
examples: Slow breathing will *calm* your heart rate.
The nurse *calmed* her before the procedure.
He sat with the boy, *calming* him until his mother arrived.
contrast: The *l* is silent: KAHM, rhyming with *palm*.

gloss: To watch or measure something regularly over a period of time.
examples: They *monitor* his blood pressure every hour.
The clinic *monitored* her heart for three days.
She is being *monitored* for side effects.

gloss: To test a large group of healthy people in order to find a disease early.
examples: They *screen* everyone over fifty for colon cancer.
The hospital *screened* two thousand people last year.
She was *screened* and cleared.

transitivity: both — transitive (test her blood), intransitive (he tested positive)
gloss: To check someone's blood, body, or ability with a medical procedure.
examples: They will *test* your blood for iron.
He *tested* positive on Monday.
She is being *tested* for allergies.
contrast: You *test* someone *for* something, and a person *tests positive* or *tests negative*.

gloss: To take a detailed picture of the inside of the body with a machine.
examples: They will *scan* your shoulder tomorrow.
The hospital *scanned* his brain twice in one night.
Her lungs are being *scanned* right now.
contrast: The *n* doubles: *scanned*, *scanning*.

gloss: To rub and press someone's muscles to relieve pain or tension.
examples: *Massage* the cream into the muscle.
She *massaged* his neck for ten minutes.
He was *massaging* his calf where it cramped.
contrast: Do not confuse *massage* /məˈsɑːʒ/ with *message* /ˈmɛsɪdʒ/, something you send.

gloss: To wash your throat by holding liquid in it and breathing out.
examples: *Gargle* with warm salt water twice a day.
He *gargled* and spat into the sink.
She has been *gargling* since her throat started hurting.
